payload.alternatives: mnema query first (ADR 01a1f11f-030f): useful but does not close a per-host gap; moves to after the layer. No large delivery in 0.1.11: leaves the VS Code and Cursor rule channel gap open another version.
payload.rationale: The delivery layer fixes the rule channel in VS Code and Cursor, where ADR-656 (nothing exclusive to Claude Code) presses hardest, and reuses the per-host hooks work of 0.1.11's delivery 8.
payload.title: 0.1.11 opens with the delivery layer, starting in VS Code (decision 01a1f10c-8c27), ahead of mnema query; Cursor and the after-the-fact shell writes follow the layer, as already decided

payload.alternatives: At the end of a session: only where the host has such a hook; the others would publish only by hand. Daily: needs a scheduler outside mnema. No trigger yet: leaves the switch with nothing to fire it.
payload.rationale: A trigger in the write itself needs no host hook, so every host behaves the same (ADR-656); a session-end hook exists only on some hosts and a daily timer needs a scheduler mnema does not have.
payload.title: The automatic publication of the public record (behind its machine switch, off by default, always through a pull request: ADR-92, ADR-617) fires when the public tree holds N unpublished events, checked in the act of writing, so it works the same on every host

payload.alternatives: Keep it private until someone asks: no demand signal yet, and the CLI and MCP already serve; turned down by the maintainer.

A typed library lets Node and TypeScript tools record without shelling out.
payload.title: @mnema/sdk is published to npm in 0.1.11, with a method to retract a link and a headless CI example that uses it

payload.alternatives: Filter and --offset together: --offset was deferred until asked. Neither: keeps the jq workaround.
payload.rationale: Study scripts today read the tail with jq to find what one agent or key wrote; a filter at the reader serves them on every host through both doors. ADR 01a1f9f6-4ccd already keeps --offset for when someone asks.
payload.title: mnema search and the MCP search tool gain a filter by the agent (--agent <name>) and by the signing key (--key <fingerprint>) in 0.1.11; --offset past 200 stays out until asked

payload.alternatives: No format change in 0.1.11: keeps the readers asymmetric and the served rule unnamed. Only witnessed in Python: leaves the other two for later.
payload.rationale: The two readers should require the same levels; naming the rule in channel.served makes what was served checkable against what governed; admitting a foreign tail opens the record to work that began elsewhere. Each is a format change and goes through the desenhar path with both readers and the published vectors.
payload.title: 0.1.11 changes the format in three places: the Python reader offers --require witnessed like the TypeScript one, channel.served names the rule it served, and a record can admit a tail of another record

payload.alternatives: Python-2.0 on the general allow list: any future package under it would pass unseen. Dropping subset-font for subsets made once and committed: no new dependency, but the brand script's check could no longer regenerate the fonts.
payload.rationale: The maintainer chose it on 2026-11-21: "Exceção só para o argparse (Recomendado)". Python-2.0 is a permissive, OSI-approved license. argparse ships in no published package. The workflow says adding a license is a decision and not a way to make a red go, so the narrowest form is an exception for one package by its purl.
payload.title: The dependency review accepts argparse@2.0.1 (Python-2.0) by name only, as a development dependency brought in by subset-font through wawoff2; the list of allowed licenses stays as it is for every other package

payload.alternatives: Sizing it with CSS on the site, as ADR-487 said: a second mechanism beside the README's, and the forced-height rule that squeezed it is exactly what a CSS route keeps reintroducing. Keeping 20 on the site: Codex reads as a dot.
payload.rationale: This restates ADR-487 with the site's half as built in mnema.work#19. ADR-487 said the site would size the mark optically with CSS. Instead the site sets the shown height on the element, as the README does, and a guard refuses any stylesheet rule that fixes a host image's size, since a forced 20 px rule had squeezed the Blossom to a dot. The README's reasons stand: the Blossom draws its mark between about 175 and 541 of its 716-unit box, the vendor's file stays untouched, and the other marks fill their boxes.
payload.title: Codex is shown in the README's hosts table by OpenAI's Blossom mark from OpenAI's own logo kit, black on a light page and white on a dark one, unmodified, with its source and sha256 in assets/hosts/SOURCES.md, at height 40 where every other host is at 20, because the mark fills about half of its own box; the site's hosts strip shows it the same way, at height 40 set on the element, with no stylesheet rule fixing the size of a host's image

payload.alternatives: [{"option": "Widen the allow-list with Python-2.0, PSF-2.0 and the inspector's text", "reason": "would let any future package under those licenses in without a decision"}, {"option": "Drop the MCP Inspector job and accept only the Python tools", "reason": "loses the only check that a real MCP client reads the served tools"}, {"option": "Leave the check red", "reason": "a red that stays on every pull request teaches everyone to ignore it"}]
payload.rationale: They come in with the CI guards of 0.1.11 (hash-pinned Python tools and the MCP Inspector job) and never ship in a package. Their licenses, read at the source: mypy MIT (three mypyc files PSF-2.0), typing-extensions PSF-2.0, @modelcontextprotocol/inspector MIT and Apache-2.0 (its LICENSE describes the transition; docs CC-BY-4.0), skills-ref Apache-2.0 (the tool did not detect it). Accepting by name, as ADR-686 did for argparse, keeps the check meaningful for every other package.
payload.title: The dependency review accepts by name four CI-only packages: mypy, typing-extensions, @modelcontextprotocol/inspector and skills-ref; the list of allowed licenses stays as it is

payload.alternatives: [{"option": "Keep 'private ADR-n' in the brief (ADR-236 as written)", "reason": "two spellings for one fact, and each new surface has to pick one"}, {"option": "Spell every label with its scope, public included", "reason": "noise on the common case: a public rule is the default reading"}]
payload.rationale: The brief wrote 'private ADR-n' while readLabel and the other surfaces wrote the scope as a suffix, and the session journal's labels added it only on a collision. One spelling, read from one function, is what a reader and a test can hold; the label still never shows a private rule as a bare ADR-n of the public chain, which is what ADR-236 protected.
payload.title: A private rule's label has one spelling everywhere, 'ADR-n (private)': the session-opening text, the session journal's labels and the pages say it the same way

payload.alternatives: [{"option": "Leave the findings open", "reason": "permanent noise that hides a real finding"}, {"option": "Pin the host versions in a lockfile", "reason": "the contract would stop testing what users install"}]
payload.rationale: Pinning either would defeat what it tests: the first installs the package this run built, the second follows the host's stable or latest release on purpose and verifies it in the same step. Dismissing with the reason written keeps the Security tab honest instead of leaving two findings open forever.
payload.title: The two Scorecard 'unpinned dependency' findings on installs that are the test itself are dismissed with their reason: run.sh's npm i -g of the tarball just packed, and host-contract's install of each host at the version chosen and checked against the vendor's signature at run time
